abstract.p: This elegy on the death of Queen Anne describes how the season appears to have turned to spring too early, with flowers blooming as if it were May rather than March. It then makes clear that it is still March, and accounts for the premature season through a conceit in which the earth takes the mourners’ tears for the showers that bring about spring. This is followed by a contrasting idea, in which the earth, described “masking in green,” appears to reject or counter human mourning in black. The poem then rejects these explanations and redefines Anne, the “flower of queens”, as the “queen of flowers,” so that the birds are imagined as singing to her. In the final lines, this is qualified: if the birds understood human grief, they would say that her “too soon” death has made a “too soon” spring; continued cries and tears, again figured as showers, are expected to mar their song and drown the flowers.

app.lem: On the same who died March 1 2

lg.l: Tis not yet may, nor yet are Aprill showrs,
And wee admire the Springs so early prime;
And cause wee see in feilds the smiling flowers,
Write Month of May, two months befor the time:
But windy March still rounds it in our eares
That earth is suer sure mistaken in our teares
Yea rather proude of our illustrious Queene
(Whom wee alas no longer time can keepe)
And cause wee morne in blacke wee will maske in greene,

And smile the while shee sees us
throobb and weepe.
Or if not soe no t r teares are tooke for showers
The Flower of Queens is then the Queene of Flowers.
Faire Queene of Flowers to thee the birds do sing;
But did they know their our greifs would weeping say
Thy too soone ashes makes make too soone a Spring,
Befor the month of Aprill and of May:
For ear'e may comes come , our Cries, Teares Aprill showers
Will marr their tunes, and drowne the smiling flowers.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Anne of Denmark, queen consort of James I, died unexpectedly on 2 March 1619 at Hampton Court after a period of ill health. Her death prompted a wave of elegiac writing that, while less intense than that following the death of her son, Prince Henry, nonetheless reflects broader national anxieties and the developing conventions of mourning royal figures in the early Stuart period.(Doelman 2016)
